Where is Cheyenne and how is the city laid out?

Cheyenne is the capital of Wyoming and the county seat of Laramie County, in the far southeast corner of the state. It sits at about 6,086 feet above sea level on Crow Creek and Dry Creek, and covers a little over 32 square miles.

Two interstates meet southwest of town. I-25 runs north to south and I-80 runs east to west, and I-180 loops through the city along US 85. Cheyenne Regional Airport offers daily nonstop United Express flights to Denver, and local buses run through the Cheyenne Transit Program. A seller here is rarely more than a few minutes from a major road, which matters when a buyer asks about commute times.

The city has several historic districts, and homes inside them may face extra review:

  • Downtown Cheyenne Historic District
  • Lakeview Historic District
  • Rainsford Historic District
  • Capitol North Historic District
  • South Side Historic District

If your house sits inside one of these areas, ask the city's Planning and Development office what applies before you spend money on repairs.

What is the short history of Cheyenne?

The Union Pacific Railroad platted Cheyenne on July 5, 1867, and the first train rolled in on November 14 of that year. The city has been Wyoming's only capital since it was named the temporary territorial capital on May 7, 1869.

Fort D. A. Russell was founded in September 1867 and later became Francis E. Warren Air Force Base in October 1949. That base is one of the oldest continuously active military installations in the country, and it still shapes the housing market through transfers and deployments.

Wyoming became a state on July 10, 1890.

What drives the Cheyenne economy?

Government, transportation, the military and a growing technology sector carry the Cheyenne economy. State offices, Union Pacific and BNSF rail yards, and F.E. Warren Air Force Base are long-standing anchors.

Newer names have joined them. Wyoming's business council lists Microsoft, Meta, Magpul, Searing Industries and Eagle Claw as major employers, and reports combined data center investment from Meta and Microsoft of more than $1.8 billion. Cheyenne Regional, the local hospital, reports more than 2,000 employees, and a Veterans Affairs medical center also serves the area.

Here is how those facts line up:

Sellers who work for the base or a large employer may need to move on a short timeline. A transfer or a job change can leave a short window to sell.

How does Cheyenne's weather affect a house?

Cheyenne is cold and semiarid, with strong summer thunderstorms, and hail is the weather that does the most harm to a roof. The National Weather Service reports that Cheyenne sees more than 6 days a year with severe hail of an inch or larger nearby, with June the busiest month and July next.

Quarter-size hail is the most commonly reported size. Hail can fall anywhere from March into October, and most reports come late in the afternoon.

The city's own climate numbers are worth knowing too:

  • Average annual precipitation is about 15.9 inches, mostly from May through August.
  • Seasonal snowfall averages about 60 inches, with March and April the snowiest months.
  • Lows reach 0 degrees Fahrenheit on roughly nine mornings a year.
  • The growing season runs about 106 days.

For a seller, this means buyers and inspectors will look closely at shingles, gutters, siding and furnace age. A roof with visible hail bruising can lower an offer or stall a financed sale. A cash buyer who purchases as-is does not ask you to fix that first.

Is flood risk a concern when selling in Cheyenne?

Flood risk is a real topic in Cheyenne because of the flash flood of August 1, 1985. The National Weather Service recorded 6.06 inches of rain in about three hours, 12 deaths, 70 injuries and more than $61 million in damage.

After the flood, a FEMA report called for better stormwater and floodplain management, and the city adopted new drainage plans and retention projects in the late 1980s. Today the city's Engineering Services Department keeps flood insurance rate maps and base flood elevations. You can reach it at 2101 O'Neil Ave., Room 206, or by phone at (307) 637-6268.

If your home is near Crow Creek or Dry Creek, check the map before you list. A buyer's lender may require flood insurance, and finding that out late can cost you days.

Which Cheyenne permits and code rules matter before a sale?

The City of Cheyenne requires a permit for many repairs sellers consider, including reroofing, decks, garages, water heaters, and electrical, plumbing and HVAC work. Permit review can take up to 10 business days, and fees are based on project value.

Some smaller jobs are exempt. A detached shed under 200 square feet needs no permit, and flatwork such as a concrete patio generally does not, unless it is in the city right-of-way. Fences over 6 feet need a permit, and the city limits fences to 4 feet in front of the house.

  • Carports over 200 square feet, or attached to another structure, need a permit.
  • Zoning violations can carry fines of $100 per day.
  • Structures built in a setback may have to be removed.

Cheyenne treats short-term rentals like other residential uses, so there is no separate registration, but each rental must hold the approvals it needs. If you have an unpermitted deck, shed or carport, call the Building Department at (307) 637-6265 before a buyer finds it in an inspection.

When are Laramie County property taxes due?

Laramie County property taxes are due in two halves, with the first half payable by November 10 and the second half payable by May 10 of the following year. If you pay the whole bill by December 31, interest on the first half is waived.

Taxes not paid by the payable date become delinquent, and delinquent taxes accrue interest at 18 percent per year. If a bill is still unpaid on May 11, the treasurer certifies a delinquent list, and the county holds a lien that can lead to a tax sale. The Laramie County Treasurer is at 309 W. 20th Street, Cheyenne.

Property is assessed to the owner of record on January 1. If you bought or recorded a deed after that date, the notice may not carry your name, but you are still responsible for the tax. The assessor mails schedules no later than the fourth Monday in April, and you have 30 days from the mailing to file a written objection. Our Wyoming property tax guide covers appeals in more detail.

What happens at closing and recording in Cheyenne?

A deed for a Cheyenne sale is recorded with the Laramie County Clerk, and the clerk cannot accept it until a sworn statement of the price and terms is filed. Wyoming law, W.S. 34-1-142, makes that statement confidential, so the sale price does not become a public record.

The clerk's recording fee is $12 for the first page and $3 for each additional page, and documents with several legal descriptions carry an added $15.50 administrative fee. The office is at 309 W 20th St, Suite 1600, and takes e-recording through several vendors. Hours are Monday through Friday, 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM.

How does a cash sale work for a Cheyenne homeowner?

A cash sale means a buyer purchases your house without a lender, so the deal does not depend on an appraisal or loan approval. You tell us about the property, we review it, and you decide whether the offer works for you.

This route often suits sellers who face one of these situations:

  • An inherited house that needs probate paperwork and cleanout.
  • A hail-damaged roof or older systems that would fail a lender's inspection.
  • A military or job move with a fixed date.
  • Back taxes or a payment problem that is getting worse.

We buy as-is, with no commission and no closing costs charged to you, and you owe nothing if you decline an offer. Call or text (424) 435-2326 or use the form on this page to start.

More questions about Cheyenne, WY

How fast can I sell my house in Cheyenne?

A cash sale can close faster than a listing because it skips lender approval and appraisal. The exact timeline depends on title work, any probate, and the date you choose. Tell us your deadline and we will work around it.

Do I need to fix hail damage before selling in Cheyenne?

No, not if you sell to a cash buyer who purchases as-is. If you list on the open market, a hail-damaged roof often comes up in the inspection and can lower the offer or require repairs. Note that reroofing needs a City of Cheyenne permit.

Is my sale price public in Wyoming?

No. The sworn statement of consideration filed with the deed is confidential under W.S. 34-1-142 and is not a public record. The county uses it for statistical purposes.

When are property taxes due in Laramie County?

Half is payable by November 10 and half by May 10 of the next year. Interest on the first half is waived if you pay the full bill by December 31, and delinquent taxes accrue 18 percent interest per year.

Who do I call about a permit or a flood map in Cheyenne?

Call the Building Department at (307) 637-6265 for permits and Engineering Services at (307) 637-6268 for flood maps and base flood elevations. Planning and Development at (307) 637-6282 handles zoning, fences and setbacks.

Where is Casper and what is around it?

Casper is in east-central Wyoming on the North Platte River and is the county seat of Natrona County. The city sits at roughly 5,100 feet and covers about 27 square miles.

Interstate 25 is the main route in and out, approaching from the north and east, and US 20/26 runs near the airport on the west side. Casper-Natrona County International Airport has United Express and Delta Connection service. Several smaller communities touch the city limits, so a Casper address may sit in a different jurisdiction than you expect:

  • Mills
  • Evansville
  • Bar Nunn
  • Unincorporated areas such as Allendale, Dempsey Acres and Red Buttes

Before you list or sell, confirm whether your parcel is inside the City of Casper or in the county. That decides who issues permits and who enforces nuisance rules.

What is the history of Casper?

Casper began when the railroad reached the site in June 1888, and residents petitioned for incorporation in April 1889. The town took its name from Fort Caspar, which honored Lt. Caspar Collins, who was killed nearby in 1865.

Oil shaped the city. Casper's first refinery was built in 1895, the oil boom ran from about 1910 into the mid-1920s, and by 1922 the Midwest Refinery was described as the largest in the world by gasoline volume. The population jumped from 2,639 in 1910 to 11,447 in 1920.

Boom and bust followed. The Texaco refinery closed in 1982 and the Amoco refinery in 1991, and the population fell from 51,016 in 1980 to 46,742 in 1990.

What does the Casper economy look like today?

Casper is a regional center for banking, commerce and energy, and it also leans on healthcare, manufacturing and tourism. Oil, gas, mining and wind power are foundational sectors, according to the city's economic development partner, Advance Casper.

Casper Mountain, the Hogadon ski area and the North Platte River support outdoor tourism. The airport is Wyoming's only Foreign Trade Zone, and a Sinclair refinery operates in nearby Evansville.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported a mean hourly wage of $28.93 in the Casper metro in May 2025, compared with $33.54 nationally. Here are the largest occupation groups it listed:

Occupation groupShare of local jobsMean hourly wage
Office and administrative support10.6%$22.84
Food preparation and serving9.8%$15.21

Transportation and material moving9.4%$24.84
Construction and extraction8.1%$28.98

Energy and construction jobs make up a large part of local work, so a slowdown can strain an owner's budget. A missed payment can turn into a sale decision.

How does Casper's climate affect a house?

Casper has long, cold, dry winters and hot, mostly dry summers, so heating systems and roofs take the most wear. The normal January high is 35.2 degrees Fahrenheit and the normal July high is 89.0.

  • Average annual snowfall is about 71.8 inches.
  • Average annual precipitation is 12.22 inches.
  • Highs reach 90 degrees on about 38 days a year.
  • Lows drop to 0 degrees on about 15 nights a year.

Snow can be extreme. In the storm of April 3 and 4, 2023, Casper recorded 26.7 inches of snow in a day and 37.4 inches over two days, both records. After a roof collapsed at a commercial building, the Natrona County building official listed warning signs for owners to watch: creaking, visible sagging, cracked or split wood members, cracks in walls and doors that pop open.

If your roof, ceilings or walls show any of those signs, a buyer's inspector will find them. A cash buyer who purchases as-is will still look at them, but you will not have to repair them before closing.

Does Casper have flood or burn scar risk?

Parts of Casper can see flash flooding, especially downstream from the slopes of Casper Mountain. On July 29, 2013, the National Weather Service issued a flash flood warning for the east side of Casper after heavy rain fell on a recent burn scar from the Sheep Herder Hill fire.

Several homes along the Clear Fork of Muddy Creek were damaged, and flooding was reported on East Second Street between Wyoming Blvd. and Hat 6 Road. Much of that day's rainfall came in about 20 minutes.

If your home is on the east side or near a creek, check flood maps and ask your insurer about coverage before a buyer's lender does. Tell a buyer about any past water problem up front.

What permits and code rules apply to Casper sellers?

The City of Casper requires building permits for most projects, and it has adopted the 2021 International Codes, including the building, residential, fire, plumbing, mechanical and fuel gas codes. Amendments are in Title 15 of the municipal code.

Small jobs have different rules. Sheds under 120 square feet do not need a building permit, and a fence not over 6 feet high needs a fence permit but not a building permit. Platforms and walkways not more than 30 inches above grade are exempt from the building permit, while taller decks likely are not.

The Code Enforcement Division handles nuisance complaints. Typical issues include:

  • Weeds and overgrowth
  • Litter and accumulated junk
  • Junk vehicles
  • Dangerous buildings
  • Recreational vehicle parking

The city notifies the owner or tenant first and asks for a correction. If the problem is not fixed, the case may be referred to Municipal Court. Residents file complaints through the Casper 311 online form.

When are Natrona County property taxes due?

Wyoming property taxes are due in two halves, with the first half payable by November 10 and the second half payable by May 10 of the following year. Paying the full amount by December 31 avoids interest and penalty on the first half under the statute.

Taxes still unpaid on May 11 are declared delinquent, and the county treasurer then demands payment. Natrona County offers an online payment portal that asks for your bill number, tax year, last name and total tax bill. The county's main office is at 200 N Center, Casper, and the phone is 307-235-9200.

Because the tax follows the property, an unpaid bill can surface at closing. Check your balance before you sign a contract. Our Wyoming property tax guide explains the appeal process.

What should Casper sellers know about the deed and sale price?

A deed for a Casper sale must come with a sworn statement of the full price and terms, and Wyoming law keeps that statement confidential. Under W.S. 34-1-142, the county clerk cannot record the deed until the statement is filed.

The statement is not a public record, and the county may use it only for statistical sales-price ratios. Transfers such as foreclosure sales and certain gifts between family members are exempt from the price disclosure.

For recording fees and procedures, call the Natrona County main office at 307-235-9200, since the county page we reviewed does not list the clerk's fees.

How does a cash sale work for a Casper homeowner?

A cash sale means we buy your house without a lender, so the sale does not hinge on a bank appraisal or loan approval. You share a few details about the home, we review them, and you decide whether to accept.

We buy as-is, with no commission and no closing costs charged to you, and you owe nothing if you turn the offer down. This option can fit a house with an old roof, deferred repairs, a code enforcement notice, or an estate that needs to be settled. Call or text (424) 435-2326, or fill out the form on this page.

More questions about Casper, WY

Can I sell a Casper house with a code violation?

Yes. A cash buyer can purchase a house that has open nuisance or permit issues, and we buy as-is. If you list the home instead, expect buyers to ask about notices from the Code Enforcement Division and about any unpermitted work.

Do I need a permit to replace a deck or fence in Casper?

Usually yes for a fence, since a fence permit is required even when the fence is not over 6 feet high. Decks not more than 30 inches above grade are exempt from the building permit, but taller ones likely need one. Confirm with the Building / Inspection Division.

When are property taxes due in Natrona County?

Half is payable by November 10 and half by May 10 of the next year. Bills unpaid on May 11 are delinquent. You can pay through the Natrona County online portal.

Is my sale price public in Wyoming?

No. The sworn statement of price filed with the deed is confidential under W.S. 34-1-142. Certain transfers, such as foreclosure sales, are exempt from the statement.

Does heavy snow damage matter when selling in Casper?

It can. Casper averages about 71.8 inches of snow a year, and the April 2023 storm set records. Buyers' inspectors look for sagging, cracks and roof wear, and a cash buyer who purchases as-is does not require those repairs first.

Gillette at a glance

Where is Gillette, Wyoming, and how is the city laid out?

Gillette is the county seat of Campbell County, in northeastern Wyoming, sitting in the Powder River Basin between the Bighorn Mountains to the west and the Black Hills to the east. The elevation is about 4,554 feet.

The city grew outward in stages. On January 1, 2018, Gillette annexed the Antelope Valley-Crestview area, which brought a large residential district inside city limits. Subdivisions such as Westover and Foothills, along with the Westover Road corridor, are part of the built-up area.

For a seller, the boundary matters more than it sounds. A house inside the city follows city zoning, city permits and city water and sewer rules. A house just outside it falls under Campbell County instead. The city planning staff say owners can petition to annex land that touches city limits, and service extensions are generally at the owner's expense.

How did Gillette start, and how fast has it grown?

Gillette began in 1891 as a railway town on the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad and was incorporated on January 6, 1892. It was named for Edward Gillette, a surveyor for the railroad company. Earlier names included Donkey Town and Rocky Pile.

A fire in November 1895 destroyed most of the young town. Growth came much later, tied to energy development. The population was 3,580 in 1960, 7,194 in 1970, 19,646 in 2000 and 33,403 in the 2020 census.

Most of that growth is recent, so Gillette has few very old houses. Sellers with homes from the growth decades should check the age of the roof, furnace and water heater before listing.

What drives the Gillette economy?

Coal, oil and coalbed methane gas have driven Gillette's economy for decades. Wyoming supplies close to 35 percent of the coal mined in the country, and much of it comes out of the Powder River Basin around Gillette.

A 2021 WyoFile report described how tied the county is to coal. Coal made up about 51.6 percent of Campbell County's assessed value in 2021, down from 58.6 percent in 2017, and assessed valuation fell by $850 million from 2020 to 2021. The same report said the two Arch Resources mines then employed 1,070 miners, and that Gillette College and the county were working on carbon technology, an industrial park and youth sports events to broaden the base.

Those numbers are from 2021, so check current figures. When mine employment or coal prices shift, local demand for houses can shift with it, and a seller who must move quickly may face a thinner pool of buyers.

  • Gillette is a regional center for media, education, health and arts, per its Wikipedia profile.
  • Wyoming's coal output matters nationally, so state and federal energy policy can reach Gillette household incomes.
  • Campbell County Memorial Hospital has 90 acute-care beds and is a certified area trauma hospital.

What does Gillette weather do to a house?

Gillette has cold winters, hot dry summers and enough hail to matter for roofs. The mean daily maximum in January is about 36 degrees Fahrenheit and the mean daily minimum is about 16. In July the mean maximum is about 86. The record high is 110 degrees and the record low is minus 40.

Annual precipitation averages about 17.6 inches, and annual snowfall averages about 55.7 inches. May is the wettest month, which lines up with the spring storm season.

On May 26, 2010, a hail storm moved through Gillette and hit the Westover and Foothills subdivisions hardest. The Gillette News-Record estimated the damage could top $46 million, including $28 million for roofs and gutters. Buyers in Gillette tend to look closely at roof age and gutters.

Freeze and thaw cycles also matter. Old windows, thin attic insulation and poor grading are worth checking before a buyer does.

Which schools, airport and transit serve Gillette?

Public schools in Gillette belong to Campbell County School District Number 1, which runs Campbell County High School and Thunder Basin High School. Gillette College, a two-year college, is also in town.

Northeast Wyoming Regional Airport has United flights operated by SkyWest, with about six daily flights to Denver. Jefferson Lines provides intercity bus service.

What permits and zoning rules affect a Gillette house sale?

Most structural work in Gillette needs a building permit and a zoning permit, and unpermitted work can complicate a sale. City planning staff say a garage or addition needs both after review by Building Inspection and Planning. Decks, sheds and retaining walls usually need both as well. A shed under 200 square feet or a retaining wall under 4 feet tall needs only the zoning permit.

Other city rules that show up in sales:

  • Fences need a free zoning permit. Front-yard fences are limited to 4 feet and side and rear fences to 6 feet.
  • Single-family zones allow only one residence per lot, so a second dwelling on the property is not permitted.
  • Homes need at least two paved off-street parking spaces.
  • Home businesses in residential zones need a Home Occupation Permit from Code Compliance.

You can look up zoning by calling the Planning Division at (307) 686-5281. Building Division contact is (307) 686-5200 or gillette@gillettewy.gov, and permits and inspections go through the city's online portal. If you inherit or buy a house that has a converted garage, an unpermitted deck or a rental unit in the basement, find out early whether the work can be legalized or whether a buyer will need to discount for it.

When are Campbell County property taxes due, and what exemptions exist?

Campbell County follows the state calendar. The first installment of the current year's tax is due September 1 and becomes delinquent after November 10 unless all taxes are paid by December 31. The second installment is due March 1 and becomes delinquent after May 10. The county treasurer mails tax bills on or before October 10.

Under Wyoming statute, unpaid balances accrue 18 percent annual interest. The statute text we read is a 2012 copy, so confirm current terms with the county.

Campbell County says homeowners, seniors and veterans can apply for 2027 exemptions from October 1, 2026 through March 1, 2027. The state Homeowner's Exemption removes 25 percent of taxable value on the first $1 million of fair market value for an owner-occupied primary residence, and the Long-term Homeowner's Exemption removes 50 percent on the first $3 million for owners 65 or older who have paid Wyoming residential property tax for at least 25 years. The veteran's exemption is a $6,000 reduction in assessed value, with a filing deadline of the fourth Monday in May.

If you sell during the year, ask your title company how current-year tax will be handled at closing. Offices to call: Treasurer (307) 682-7268 and Assessor (307) 682-7266.

How does a sale get recorded in Campbell County?

The Campbell County Clerk records deeds and keeps the grantor and grantee indexes. Under Wyoming Statute 18-3-402, the clerk stamps each instrument with the day, hour and minute it arrives, and the date of record is the filing date. The clerk will not record a document until the fee is paid. The Clerk's office phone is (307) 682-7285.

The Gillette planning FAQ also advises buyers to read the title report for easements, pre-annexation agreements and deed restrictions. A seller can save time by pulling the plat and any recorded agreements before listing.

If the house came through an estate, the paperwork that gives someone authority to sign the deed has to be in order before closing, so start that early.

What do Gillette sellers usually face, and how does a cash sale fit?

Gillette sellers commonly face aging roofs, deferred repairs, estate transfers and job moves. A cash sale works well when the owner wants to skip showings, repairs and a long financing contingency.

A cash offer from a company like ours is based on the house as it stands. We look at condition, location and the work a buyer would take on, and then we make an offer for you to accept or decline. There is no obligation, and we do not promise a specific price before we see the property.

  • Open-market listing: more exposure and often a higher price, with agent commission, repairs, showings and a financing timeline.
  • Cash sale: faster and simpler, usually at a lower price than a fully prepared listing.

Whichever route you choose, compare the numbers. If you owe back taxes, have a lien or are behind on a mortgage, tell us early, because those items change the closing steps.

More questions about Gillette, WY

Can I sell my Gillette house if it needs a new roof?

Yes. Hail has damaged many Gillette roofs, including the May 26, 2010 storm that hit Westover and Foothills. A cash buyer prices the roof into the offer, so you do not have to replace it before selling.

When are property taxes due in Campbell County?

The first half is due September 1 and the second half March 1. Taxes become delinquent after November 10 and May 10, and paying everything by December 31 avoids interest on the first half. Call the Campbell County Treasurer at (307) 682-7268 to confirm your balance.

Do I need a permit to sell a house with an unpermitted deck or garage in Gillette?

A permit is not required to sell, but unpermitted work can slow a sale or lower offers. The city says decks, additions and garages usually need building and zoning permits. Call the Building Division at (307) 686-5200 to ask whether work can be permitted after the fact.

Where are deeds recorded for a Gillette home?

Deeds are recorded with the Campbell County Clerk. The clerk stamps the date and time each instrument arrives and requires the fee in advance. The Clerk's office number is (307) 682-7285.

Does the Wyoming homeowner exemption affect my sale?

It lowers the taxable value while you live in the house as your primary residence, but it does not stop the sale. The 2027 filing window in Campbell County runs from October 1, 2026 to March 1, 2027. Ask your title company how tax is handled at closing.

Laramie at a glance

Selling in Laramie?

Get My Cash Offer →

Where is Laramie, Wyoming, and what is the setting?

Laramie is the county seat of Albany County, in southeastern Wyoming, about 50 miles from Cheyenne and roughly 25 miles north of the Colorado line. It sits on the Laramie River at the point where Interstate 80 meets U.S. Route 287.

The city stands at about 7,165 feet on a high plain between two mountain ranges. That elevation shapes everything from heating bills to how long snow stays on a roof.

Denver is about 130 miles away, and the University of Wyoming describes Laramie as affordable compared with many college towns. Outdoor areas nearby include Vedauwoo, the Medicine Bow-Routt National Forest and the Snowy Range Ski Area.

How did Laramie begin?

Laramie dates to 1868, when the Union Pacific Railroad platted the town and began selling lots on April 20. Track reached the town on May 4, 1868, and Laramie was officially incorporated on January 13, 1874.

The railroad chose Laramie for a major repair depot with machine shops, a roundhouse and a power plant. Population jumped past 3,000 during construction, then fell to about 800 once the crews left. An 1874 rolling mill that reprocessed iron rails eventually employed 300 men.

The University of Wyoming came out of an 1880s deal that gave Cheyenne the state capital and Laramie the university. It opened in September 1887 with 40 students. Downtown and the West Side are both listed as historic districts, and Laramie has 21 sites on the National Register of Historic Places, including the Ivinson Mansion and Old Main on campus.

What drives the Laramie economy?

The University of Wyoming is Laramie's largest employer, with nearly 3,000 employees, according to the Wyoming state history encyclopedia. The same source says tourism, health care and retail together provide about as many jobs as the university.

Railroad jobs began to decline in the mid-1950s, and the university took over as the anchor. Enrollment was about 8,200 students in live instruction in fall 2024, plus nearly 2,300 online, per Wikipedia. The median age in the 2020 census was 27.2, which is young for a Wyoming city.

For sellers, that mix matters in two ways:

  • A young population means many Laramie households rent, so some sellers are landlords rather than owner-occupants.
  • The university is one large employer, so changes there can matter to local housing demand.

What does Laramie's climate mean for a house?

Laramie has a cold semi-arid climate with long, dry winters and short, warm summers. Average temperature is about 21 degrees Fahrenheit in December and 64 in July. Annual precipitation runs about 10.5 to 11 inches, and annual snowfall is about 48 to 50 inches.

The growing season is short, with freezing temperatures possible from September 14 through June 6. Record extremes run from 96 degrees in July to minus 50.

The city's building office lists local design criteria such as snow loads, wind speeds, frost depth and seismic classification in its Bulletin #2. A buyer reviewing a Laramie house will likely ask about roof condition, insulation and furnace age.

Which schools, roads and airport serve Laramie?

Albany County School District #1 is headquartered in Laramie and is the only district in the county. It operates 19 public schools, and the Laramie schools include seven elementary schools, one middle school, Laramie High School and Whiting High School. Snowy Range Academy is a K-7 charter school, and the UW Lab School covers K-9.

Interstate 80 and U.S. 287 meet in town. The business route of I-80 runs along Grand Avenue. Laramie Regional Airport is about three miles west of downtown on WYO 130, with SkyWest flying to Denver for United.

What permits and zoning rules affect a Laramie house sale?

Laramie requires a building permit for most residential projects and repairs. The city follows the 2024 International Building Code with local amendments in Laramie Municipal Code Chapter 15.24.

The Code Administration page lists work that does not need a permit:

  • One-story sheds and playhouses under 200 square feet that meet setbacks.
  • Fences up to 7 feet high in back and side yards only.
  • Retaining walls up to 4 feet high, measured from the bottom of the footing.
  • Unattached decks under 200 square feet that are no more than 30 inches above grade and do not serve the front door.
  • Painting, papering and similar finish work.

Permits are filed through the city's online Civic Access portal, and the estimated plan review period is three weeks. Code Administration is at 406 Ivinson Avenue, phone 307-721-5271.

Zoning comes from the Unified Development Code. The city lists many zoning districts and overlays, including the Aquifer Protection Overlay and the Gateway Overlay. Planning asks owners to reach out before buying property, changing a use or dividing land. The Planning Division is at 320 E Grand Avenue, (307) 721-5207, or planning@cityoflaramie.org.

If you have a converted basement, an old addition or an unpermitted deck, ask Code Administration what it would take to bring it into compliance before a buyer finds it.

When are Albany County property taxes due?

Wyoming law sets the property tax calendar for every county, including Albany County. The first half is due on or after September 1 and payable on or after November 10. The second half is due on or after March 1 and payable on or after May 10 of the following year. Paying the full amount by December 31 avoids interest and penalty.

Unpaid balances accrue interest at 18 percent per year. The statute text we read is a 2012 copy, so confirm the current terms with the county.

The Albany County Treasurer's number is 307-721-2502, and the Assessor's is 307-721-2511. The county has an online tax portal for looking up and paying bills. The county courthouse is at 525 E Grand Avenue.

Wyoming's Homeowner's Exemption removes 25 percent of taxable value on the first $1 million of fair market value for a primary residence. The Long-term Homeowner's Exemption removes 50 percent on the first $3 million for owners 65 or older with at least 25 years of Wyoming residential property tax payments. For tax year 2027, the owner must live in the home at least eight months of the year. The County Assessor reviews each application.

How is a Laramie sale recorded?

Deeds in Albany County are recorded with the County Clerk, which is Kayla White's office at 307-721-2541. Under Wyoming Statute 18-3-402, the clerk stamps each instrument with the day, hour and minute it arrives and keeps indexes of grantors and grantees.

The date of record is the filing date, and the clerk cannot record a document until the fee is paid. Before listing, you can pull your recorded deed, any easements and any recorded agreements so a buyer sees clean paperwork.

What do Laramie sellers usually face, and when does a cash sale help?

Laramie sellers often face rental houses with deferred maintenance, estates, job moves and houses needing roof or insulation work. A cash sale helps when you want to avoid repairs, showings and a financing contingency.

A cash offer from our team is based on the house as it is. We review condition, location and the work a buyer would take on, then make an offer you can accept or decline. We do not promise a price before seeing the property.

  • Traditional listing: more exposure and often a higher price, with commission, repairs and a longer timeline.
  • Cash sale: fewer steps and a faster close, typically at a lower price than a prepared listing.

Tell us early about back taxes, liens, tenants or a mortgage balance. Those details shape the closing steps and the paperwork the title company will need.

More questions about Laramie, WY

Can I sell my Laramie house as a rental with tenants in it?

Often yes, though lease terms and timing need to be reviewed. Tell us about the lease and the move-out date so we can plan the closing.

When are Albany County property taxes due?

The first half is due September 1 and payable by November 10, and the second half is due March 1 and payable by May 10. Paying everything by December 31 avoids interest on the first half. Call the Albany County Treasurer at 307-721-2502 to confirm your balance.

Do I need a permit for work on my Laramie house before selling?

Most residential projects and repairs need a building permit, with exceptions for small sheds, low fences, short retaining walls and finish work. Contact Laramie Code Administration at 307-721-5271 before starting. You do not need a permit to sell, but unpermitted work can complicate a sale.

Where do I record a deed for a Laramie property?

Deeds are recorded with the Albany County Clerk, phone 307-721-2541. The clerk stamps the time of receipt and requires the fee up front.

Does winter affect selling a house in Laramie?

It can. Laramie averages about 48 to 50 inches of snow a year, and freezing temperatures are possible from mid-September through early June. Plan inspections and closings with winter weather in mind.
